full_judgment:
ATM Afzal CJ : The short question for consideration in this appeal by leave filed by the plaintiffs is whether the learned Judge of the High Court Division acted with any amount of reason in making an order of remand in a Second Appeal No. 1242 of 1962 for writing out a proper judgment upon consideration of evidence after 27 years of the passing of the impugned judgment which was a judgment of affirmance granting the decree in a suit for permanent injunction. We entertain no doubt whatsoever that the order of remand was wholly unreasonable and is liable to be set aside. The ordinary course could have been to send the matter back to the High Court Division for disposal of the second appeal on merit. But in that case we shall also be guilty of committing the same mistake as made by the High Court Division, for, 9 years have gone by since the date of the impugned judgment of the High Court Division. In this circumstance we ourselves considered the matter on merit and found that the concurrent decree passed in favour of the plaintiff-appellants was quite justified and there is no good reason to make an order of remand now for deciding the second appeal on merit. 

 4. Although a large number of defendants filed separate written statements, defendant No. 1 was found to be the real contestant who along with defendant No. 41 only came forward to depose. The learned Assistant Judge after an elaborate consideration of the documentary and oral evidence found title with the plaintiffs and disbelieved the defendants case both as to title and possession. Plaintiffs examined 7 witnesses in support of their possession. Having noticed the hollowness of the defendants case, that is, admittedly defendant No. 1 (main contestant) had no title and the DWs "completely failed to prove that the defendants ever possessed the suit land", the learned Assistant Judge without noting the statements of the PWs as to who said what held: 

 Under these facts and circumstances I fully accept the depositions of all the PWs 1 to 7 that the plaintiffs were and are all along in possession of the suit land. Though there are some minor discrepancies in the deposition of PWs. here and there still, under present facts and circumstances, I accept their deposition and I think they have highly satisfactorily proved that the plaintiffs are in possession of suit land through their bargadars Abul Hossain and others all along by manufacturing. salt on the suit land, as the suit lands had been converted for purpose of salt manufacture for 6/7 years and as the plaintiffs put the land to Abul Hossain and others for that purpose the attention of shrewd defendants 1 Abdul Kader and of other defendants 2 to 10 fall on the suit land and they tried to disturb plaintiff's possession in the same with help of other defendants as their attempt to have lariat of suit land under the plaintiffs was not successful. Thus I decide under present facts and circumstances and evidences on record on either side carefully, I accept plaintiffs case that the defendants, threatened them for the last time on 25-1-54 with dispossession of suit land by cutting away the embankments, by not allowing plaintiffs bargadar to manufacture salt on suit land and by burning down their khamar-houses etc. thereon. Defendants have no title and possession in suit land and, as such, the plaintiffs are entitled to have a permanent injunction against the plaintiffs as prayed for. 

 The learned lower Court had the privilege to mark the demeanors of the witnesses and he was inclined to believe that the plaintiffs are in possession of the disputed land. The documentary evidence clearly show that the plaintiffs have title over the lands. They have been paying rent from the same. The oral evidence show that the plaintiffs are in possession of the disputed lands. Though there were some minor discrepancies in the depositions of PWs. the learned lower Court accepted their depositions as satisfactory and I find nothing to disagree with him. 

 9. It appears from the impugned judgment that the learned Judge took exception for not noticing the deposition of the PWs. in details as regards possession since the suit was one for permanent injunction and even then finding possession of the plaintiffs in the suit land. The learned Judge was particularly critical of the lower appellate Court holding that a sweeping observation that it found no reason to disagree with the finding of the trial Court on possession although finding itself that the PWs were discrepant in their statements on possession cannot be said to be a finding of fact on consideration of evidence. A remand order was therefore found necessary for the purpose of arriving at finding of fact (as to possession) by the lower appellate Court. 

 10. The learned Judge quite apparently did not make the order of remand on the grounds as provided in Order XLI rules 23 and 25 but it was made under a general and inherent power of the Court. This Court observed in Probodh Ranjan Shome vs. Md Easin 1980 BSCR 457 that it is well-settled that remand orders are not to be made as a matter of course. When there is sufficient evidence on record, remand of a case to the trial Court for fresh hearing is not called for. It has been laid down since long almost uniformly that a remand order should be avoided as far as possible. The Privy Council in some cases observed that indiscriminate order of remand tantamount to shirking the responsibility vide Dr Rezia Khatun vs. Bhanu Guha and another, 1986 BLD (AD) 135. 

 11. This Court disapproved the order of remand passed in revision when no additional evidence was required and directed the High Court Division to dispose of the matter on merit. See Attor Mia vs. Mahmuda Khatun Chowdhury, 43 DLR (AD) 78. Again in the case of Hussain Ahmed Chowdhury vs. Nurul Amin, 47 DLR (AD) 162 this Court deprecated order of remand made by the High Court Division in revision in an old case of 30 years and directed it to dispose of the revision case on merit observing that if there was misreading or non-consideration of material evidence by the Courts below, it was incumbent on the revisional Court to consider the same and to arrive at a proper finding on the material evidence on record and to finally dispose of the case. 

 12. Apart from the fact that superior Courts have generally shown aversion to an order of remand except for a substantial cause, the learned Judge in this case ought to have considered that it was far more reasonable for him to look into the evidence himself to be satisfied about the correctness or otherwise of the concurrent finding of the Courts below regarding possession of the plaintiffs than to make an order of remand after 27 years of the appellate judgment. It is found that the plaintiffs drew the Court's attention to Abdus Salam and another vs. Alah Miah Serang and another, 23 DLR (SC) 12, in support of their contention that the High Court Division can itself look into the evidence under section 103 of the Code of Civil Procedure (since omitted by the Law Reforms Ordinance 1978). The learned Judge, however, ignored that decision finding that the facts of that case were different but it was over-looked that it is well-settled that since the amendment of the language of section 103 in 1926 the power of the High Court had been widened and its object was to avoid remands with their consequent delay and expense, vide Brojendra vs. Mahim 31 CWN 32. When the Court has decided a question of fact without considering material evidence on record and the evidence on record is sufficient, the High Court Division can in second appeal decide the question without making an order of remand for the said purpose. 

 14. In order to do complete justice and by way of practicing the principle preached above as to avoiding an order of remand, we ourselves looked into the evidence of the 7 PWs and feel satisfied that the evidence of possession is fully uniform coming from competent witnesses and there is no major discrepancy or infirmity in the said evidence. Mr. Sharifuddin Chaklader, learned Advocate-on-Record for respondent No. 14 could not point out anything from their evidence so as to make their evidence unreliable. He found it difficult to contend that the concurrent finding of the Courts below as regards possession by the plaintiffs, even though the depositions of the PWs were not reproduced in their judgments, was basically wrong or not sustainable.
